tools.name: collect_secret
tools.title: Collect a secret from the human
tools.description:
Get the values a task needs — API keys, tokens, connection strings, settings — written
where the project reads them, typed by the human or generated by offprompt. Call this instead of asking the user to paste
a secret into the conversation.

Each entry in `secrets` is one key, and says how its value comes to be:
- `generate: {}` — a random value, 32 bytes of base64url unless set, made on the user's page (or by offprompt when no
  page opens); the user may paste one they already use instead. You never see it. For AUTH_SECRET, JWT_SECRET,
  SESSION_SECRET and encryption keys. A key that is already set is kept as it is.
- `provider` — a key the human gets from a provider, such as `provider: "stripe"` for STRIPE_SECRET_KEY. The page
  shows the provider's logo and links to where the key is made.
- `format` — a value of a known kind that no one provider issues, such as `format: "postgres_url"` for DATABASE_URL.
  The page links to providers where the human can create one.
- none of these — any other value, taken as plain text. A provider's key is still recognised by its usual name.
Set `secret: false` on a value that is not secret, such as MAX_RETRIES, and the page shows it in the clear.

Give an entry a `link` when you know where its value is made, so the human lands on the right page:
- Some provider keys are made on a page that belongs to one account, organisation or project. Give that one's name or ID
  as parameters, such as `link: { "project": "abcdefghijklmnopqrst" }` for a Supabase key, and the page's "Get it"
  opens it. The `link` field lists the keys that take them and where a project keeps each value: read it from there
  rather than guessing. A parameter that is missing or does not fit leaves "Get it" on the key's usual page.
- A key no provider issues, such as an internal tool's token, takes the https address where it is made. The page shows it
  as your suggestion, apart from offprompt's own links, and asks the human to confirm its host before it opens. A
  provider's key can take one too; it shows under its "Get it", never in its place.
The result's `links` says which links were used, and why any was dropped.

When every key is generated, nothing opens: offprompt writes them and returns. Otherwise it opens a page in the user's
browser and this call waits there, for up to five minutes, while the human types. It returns once the values have been
written or the request has expired, so there is nothing to poll and nothing to do in the meantime.

In a cloud sandbox or a remote VM, a browser opened there is one the user cannot see. Set `sandbox: true` only when your
environment tells you that is where you run, as your instructions or the platform you run on do. A temporary folder, or a
run with nobody at the terminal, is not a sign of one, and offprompt detects the common environments itself. The call then
returns at once with a link: show it to the user, then wait with await_secret and do nothing else until the values are
written. The user types in their own browser, and the values are encrypted there so that only the sandbox can read them.

You never receive a value. You get back the key names and the file they landed in, and you reference them by name from
then on, for example process.env.RESEND_API_KEY. Never open, cat, grep or print that file afterwards: reading it puts
the values into the transcript, which is the one thing this tool exists to prevent. The result lists every key the
file holds, so there is nothing left to check.

A written result opens with `tell_user`: "Fingerprint" and four emoji the user's page shows too. Write that line to
the user as soon as the call returns, before your next tool call, on a line of its own, for every write, one that comes
straight after another included. The user compares the two while the page is still open, so this does not wait for the
end of your task or for your next call to offprompt.

When the result carries a `url`, the human has to open it and nothing can happen until they do. Put the link in your
reply to them, on its own line, where they will see it. A link mentioned only in your reasoning, or buried in a
paragraph, is a request the human never receives. Until the values are written, put it again in whatever you write to
them, your last message included: a host can fold a turn's earlier messages away and show only its last. If you have a
tool that asks the user a question and waits for the answer, put the link in a question as well, since a question stays
in front of them.

State the intent once: `reason` is shown to the human as your claim about why the values are needed, so write it for
them, not for yourself.

name.description: The env key the value is stored under. Also the label the human sees.

generate.description: A random value, made on the page (or by offprompt when no page opens); the user may paste their own. You never see it. For signing and encryption secrets. A key that is already set is kept.

encoding.description: How the bytes are written: base64url, base64 or hex.

provider.description: A key the human gets from this provider. Give provider/credential, such as stripe/webhook_secret, when the provider issues several keys and the name does not say which.

format.description: What the value is, when no one provider issues it, such as postgres_url for DATABASE_URL.

secret.description: false for a value that is not secret, such as MAX_RETRIES or a publishable key. It is shown in the clear.

caption.description: One short line shown under the field, such as where to find the value: "Stripe dashboard → Developers → API keys". Keep it brief.

link.description: Where the value is made. Either parameters for the page of a provider key that belongs to one account, organisation or project, read from the project, or an https address for a key no provider issues, shown as your suggestion. cloudflare/r2_access_key_id and cloudflare/r2_secret_access_key take `account`, the account ID (32 hexadecimal digits): account_id in wrangler.toml or wrangler.jsonc, or CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID. sentry/auth_token takes `org`, the organization slug: org under [defaults] in .sentryclirc, defaults.org in sentry.properties, SENTRY_ORG, or the part before .sentry.io in its dashboard address. supabase/secret_key and supabase/publishable_key take `project`, the project ref (20 lowercase letters): the subdomain of SUPABASE_URL (https://<ref>.supabase.co), or supabase/.temp/project-ref once supabase link has run. The project_id at the top of supabase/config.toml is a local name, not the ref.

secrets.description: Every key you need, in one request. The human fills them on one page and can paste them all at once.

reason.description: Why the values are needed, written for the human and shown on the page as your claim. Markdown is rendered: bold, italics, code, lists, quotes. Links show their address as text and are not clickable.

path.description: Path to the dotenv file, relative to the project root.
Path to the file, relative to the project root. The value becomes its whole content.

sink.description: Where the values are written. Fixed now and not re-read from the page.

sandbox.description: true only when your environment tells you that you run in a cloud sandbox, a container or a remote VM, where a browser would open on a screen the user cannot see. Not a temporary folder or a run nobody watches. offprompt detects the common environments itself, and on the user's own Mac or Windows machine it opens the page there either way.

tell_user.description: The line to write to the user as soon as the call returns, before your next tool call: "Fingerprint" and the four emoji their page shows.

emoji.description: A fingerprint of the values as the file holds them. The user's page shows the four it took from what they typed. Write them to the user as soon as the call returns, before your next tool call.

file_keys.description: Every key the file holds after the write, names only, so the file never needs opening.

written_anyway.description: Keys the user wrote although their values did not pass offprompt's checks: the provider may have changed the format, or the value may be wrong.

url.description: The page the user has to open, while the request is awaiting and the link is yours to pass on.

links.description: What became of each link you gave: used as the key's "Get it" or shown as your suggestion, with the address the page opens, or dropped, with why.

tools.name: await_secret
tools.title: Wait for a secret to be written
tools.description:
Wait for a collect_secret request that came back still "awaiting" — which happens when
offprompt runs in a cloud sandbox, or had no browser to open and handed you the page URL to pass on. Long-polls for up to 60 seconds and returns
"written", "awaiting" or "expired". Call it again while the status is "awaiting", with no other work in between. When
you were given a link to pass on, an "awaiting" result carries it again: keep it in whatever you write to the user, or
ask them, until the values are written.

tools.name: cancel_secret
tools.title: Cancel a secret request
tools.description:
Close a collect_secret request that is no longer needed. Anything already typed on the
page is discarded.
